paragraphs: By the social compact we have given the body politic existence and life. Now we must give it movement and will through legislation. The original act by which the body is formed and united does not in any way settle what it ought to do to preserve itself.

What is good and in keeping with order is so by the nature of things, independently of human conventions. All justice comes from God, who is its only source; but if we knew how to receive so high an inspiration, we would need neither government nor laws. Doubtless there is a universal justice that comes from reason alone; but to be accepted among us, this justice must be mutual. Humanly speaking, where nature provides no sanctions, the laws of justice have no effect among men. They merely benefit the wicked and harm the just, when the just man observes them toward everybody and nobody observes them toward him. Conventions and laws are therefore needed to join rights to duties and to direct justice to its object. In the state of nature, where everything is common, I owe nothing to anyone to whom I have promised nothing; I recognize as belonging to others only what is of no use to me. In the state of society all rights are fixed by law, and the case is different.

But what, after all, is a law? As long as we are content to attach purely metaphysical ideas to the word, we will go on arguing without reaching an understanding; and when we have defined a law of nature, we will be no nearer to defining a law of the State.

I have already said that there can be no general will directed at a particular object. Such an object must be either within the State or outside it. If it is outside, a will foreign to the State cannot be general in relation to it. If it is within, it is part of the State, and then a relation arises between whole and part that makes them two separate beings: the part is one, and the whole minus the part is the other. But the whole minus a part is not the whole; and while this relation lasts, there is no whole, only two unequal parts. It follows that the will of one is no longer in any respect general in relation to the other.

But when the whole people makes a decree for the whole people, it is considering only itself. If a relation is formed then, it is between two aspects of the entire object, with no division of the whole. In that case the matter on which the decree is made is general, like the will that decrees it. This act is what I call a law.

When I say that the object of laws is always general, I mean that law considers subjects _en masse_ and actions in the abstract, never a particular person or action. Thus the law may decree that there shall be privileges, but it cannot confer them on anybody by name. It may set up several classes of citizens, and even lay down the qualifications for belonging to them, but it cannot name the persons who are to belong to them. It may establish a monarchical government with hereditary succession, but it cannot choose a king or name a royal family. In a word, no function that has a particular object belongs to the legislative power.

Seen this way, it is clear at once that no one can still ask whose business it is to make laws, since they are acts of the general will. No one can ask whether the prince is above the law, since he is a member of the State; nor whether the law can be unjust, since no one is unjust to himself; nor how we can be both free and subject to the laws, since they are only registers of our wills.

We see further that, since the law unites universality of will with universality of object, what any man, whoever he is, commands on his own initiative cannot be a law. Even what the Sovereign commands about a particular matter is no nearer to being a law; it is a decree, an act not of sovereignty but of magistracy.

I therefore give the name ‘Republic’ to every State governed by laws, whatever the form of its administration may be; for only then does the public interest govern, and the _res publica_ count as a _reality_. Every legitimate government is republican;[1] I will explain later what government is.

Laws are, properly speaking, only the conditions of civil association. The people, being subject to the laws, ought to be their author; the conditions of the society ought to be set solely by those who come together to form it. But how are they to set them? By common agreement, by a sudden inspiration? Has the body politic an organ to declare its will? Who can give it the foresight to draft and announce its acts in advance? Or how is it to announce them when the need arises? How can a blind multitude, which often does not know what it wills because it rarely knows what is good for it, carry out for itself so great and difficult an enterprise as a system of legislation? Of itself the people always wills the good, but of itself it does not always see it. The general will is always right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened. The people must be made to see things as they are, and sometimes as they ought to appear to it. It must be shown the good road it is looking for, protected from the seductive influence of individual wills, taught to see times and places as a series, and made to weigh the attraction of present and visible advantages against the danger of distant and hidden evils. Individuals see the good they reject; the public wills the good it does not see. All alike need guidance. The former must be compelled to bring their wills into line with their reason; the latter must be taught to know what it wills. If that is done, public enlightenment produces a union of understanding and will in the social body: the parts work together exactly, and the whole is raised to its highest power. This makes a legislator necessary.
